lines.text: 6 gears are meshed in a row, and their teeth do not slip. The first gear turns clockwise.
Which way does the last gear turn?
Lock in your answer. Now watch what actually happens.
The last gear turns counter-clockwise, the opposite way from the first.
Two meshed gears always turn opposite ways, so every mesh flips the direction. With 6 gears there are 5 meshes. 5 flips leave one flip over, so the last gear is reversed.
An odd number of gears gives the same direction. Follow for a new puzzle every day.

lines.text: A solid sphere and a hollow sphere, with the same mass and radius, are released together at the top of the same ramp. They roll without slipping.
Which one reaches the bottom first?
Lock in your answer. Now watch what actually happens.
The solid sphere wins. It takes 1.8 seconds, against 2 seconds.

A rolling object has to spin as well as move down the ramp, and spinning takes energy. The solid sphere has more of its mass near the middle, so less energy goes into spinning and more into moving down.
Same ramp, same start, but the shape decides the race. Follow for a new puzzle every day.

lines.text: Two frictionless tracks start at the same height and end at the same height. Track B is straight. Track A dips down in the middle and climbs back up. Two balls are released together.
Which ball reaches the finish first?
Lock in your answer. Now watch what actually happens.
Ball A wins, the one on the dipped track. It takes 2.3 seconds, against 2.7 seconds for the straight one.
The dip lets the ball drop lower, so it builds up more speed. Its path is longer, but the extra speed more than makes up for it.
A longer path can be the faster path. Follow for a new puzzle every day.

lines.text: A heavy ball, 10 times heavier than a light ball, rolls at 3 meters per second and hits the light ball at rest. The collision is perfectly elastic.
How fast does the light ball shoot away?
Lock in your answer. Now watch what actually happens.
About double. It leaves at 5.5 meters per second, and the heavy ball barely slows down.
In a perfectly elastic hit, the balls separate at the same speed they approached. The heavy ball barely slows down, so the light ball must leave about one full speed faster than it.
A heavy ball can launch a light one at nearly twice its own speed. Follow for a new puzzle every day.
